detectors.why_it_matters: msg.value is the value of the whole call, so every iteration credits the caller with the same ether. A caller that loops over a list of recipients receives far more than they sent, and the contract pays the difference out of its own balance.
detectors.how_to_fix: Take the value out of the loop: divide msg.value by the number of recipients up front and pay each one a share, or require the caller to send one value per recipient and check it against msg.value in total.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the loop body never pays anything out and msg.value is only read for a check that does not change per iteration.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: msg.value; Slither documentation: msg.value in a loop detector

detectors.title: The contract has more than one constructor
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a constructor and inherits one from a base contract.
detectors.why_it_matters: Only one of them runs, and which one depends on the inheritance order and on how the arguments are threaded through. The contract that is deployed on chain is then not necessarily the contract the developer read, and the state it initialises is not necessarily the state that was designed.
detectors.how_to_fix: Keep one constructor in the most derived contract and have it call the base constructors with explicit arguments, so the initialisation order is visible in one place.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless when the base constructor does nothing but the derived one does the real initialisation, and the argument threading is unambiguous.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: inheritance and constructors; Slither documentation: multiple constructors detector

detectors.title: The contract reuses the name of a well-known contract
detectors.what_it_means: The contract's name matches a name that other, unrelated contracts also use.
detectors.why_it_matters: Users recognise contracts by name. Two contracts with the same name and different addresses is exactly the shape of a substitution attack: a user who checks the name rather than the address believes they are holding or interacting with the contract they meant.
detectors.how_to_fix: Give the contract a distinctive name that no other contract uses, and make sure the interface the user sees shows the address as well.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the contract is internal, is never presented to a user, or shares its name with a contract that is genuinely the same code.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: contract name reused detector

detectors.title: A retryable transaction is not checked against the last attempt
detectors.what_it_means: The contract handles a retryable transaction without comparing the incoming attempt hash with the last one it recorded.
detectors.why_it_matters: A retry that arrives after a newer attempt can be applied out of order, so an old state transition lands on top of a newer one. The result is a transaction executed with stale intent, and the contract's own record of what happened no longer matches the chain.
detectors.how_to_fix: Record the hash of each attempt and refuse an attempt whose hash is not the one expected, so only the latest attempt is applied.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the contract's logic is idempotent, so applying an older attempt changes nothing.
detectors.references: Optimism documentation: retryable transactions; Slither documentation: out-of-order retryable detector

detectors.title: A state variable can be written without permission
detectors.what_it_means: The contract writes to a state variable that looks like it should be under access control, from a path that has none.
detectors.why_it_matters: A variable that holds an owner, an admin, a pause flag or a fee is written without a check. Anyone who can reach that path sets it, and the contract's own protections are turned off by the person they were meant to exclude.
detectors.how_to_fix: Route every write to that variable through a single guarded function, and check the caller there rather than at each call site.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the write happens only in the constructor, or only on a path that is itself unreachable without permission.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: access control; Slither documentation: unprotected variables detector

detectors.title: A public getter hides part of what it returns
detectors.what_it_means: The contract exposes a public mapping to a struct that contains a dynamic array.
detectors.why_it_matters: The compiler-generated getter returns only the first element of the array. A caller -- a front end, an indexer, another contract -- that reads the getter sees one entry while the contract holds many, so a list that should be full looks empty and a list that should hold one entry hides the rest.
detectors.how_to_fix: Do not rely on the generated getter: expose an explicit function that returns the whole array, or a count and an indexed accessor.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the struct's array is never read through the getter, or where the contract's own logic always reads storage directly.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: public state variables; Slither documentation: public mappings with nested variables detector

detectors.title: A deprecated Pyth function is used
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls a Pyth function that has been deprecated.
detectors.why_it_matters: A deprecated function is kept for compatibility and returns an answer it no longer stands behind -- typically without the same validity guarantees. The contract prices against an answer the network does not vouch for, and the call may stop working when the deprecation is finally carried out.
detectors.how_to_fix: Move to the current Pyth interface, and check the returned price's confidence and publish time as part of the same change.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the deprecated function is called on a path the contract never exercises, or where the deprecation notice explicitly says the behaviour is unchanged.
detectors.references: Pyth documentation: deprecated functions; Slither documentation: pyth deprecated functions detector

detectors.title: The confidence of a Pyth price is not checked
detectors.what_it_means: The contract uses a Pyth price without looking at the width of its confidence interval.
detectors.why_it_matters: A wide confidence interval means the network does not agree on the price. Using it anyway means the contract trades at a price that the price network itself flags as uncertain, and the loss lands on whichever side of the trade the market moves.
detectors.how_to_fix: Compare the returned confidence against a threshold and refuse the price when it is too wide, with the threshold set for the size of the trade.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the price is only used for reporting, or where the size traded is small enough that the uncertainty cannot be material.
detectors.references: Pyth documentation: price feeds and confidence; Slither documentation: pyth unchecked confidence detector

detectors.title: The age of a Pyth price is not checked
detectors.what_it_means: The contract uses a Pyth price without checking when it was published.
detectors.why_it_matters: An old price is still a valid answer. If the market has moved and the feed has not published, the contract trades at yesterday's price, and the counterparty -- not the contract -- absorbs the difference.
detectors.how_to_fix: Require the returned publish time to be within the window the operation tolerates, and revert when it is not.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the operation is deliberately based on a slow-moving price, or where the price is only used for reporting.
detectors.references: Pyth documentation: price feeds and publish time; Slither documentation: pyth unchecked publish time detector

detectors.title: A base constructor runs twice
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls the same base constructor more than once, or passes the same arguments to two bases that share state.
detectors.why_it_matters: The initialisation runs twice. The second run overwrites what the first wrote, so the deployed state depends on the order of the calls rather than on what the code reads like, and any value set in the first call is silently replaced.
detectors.how_to_fix: Call each base constructor exactly once, and give each base its own arguments so the order cannot matter.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the base constructor is genuinely called once and Slither cannot see the second call through a modifier or an internal function.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: inheritance and constructor arguments; Slither documentation: reused constructor detector

detectors.title: Assembly returns instead of leaving the block
detectors.what_it_means: Inline assembly uses return where the intent was leave.
detectors.why_it_matters: return exits the whole call frame; leave exits only the current block. The code after the intended exit therefore still runs, so a branch that was supposed to stop does not stop, and the function's result and its side effects both differ from what was written.
detectors.how_to_fix: Use leave to exit a Yul block, and reserve return for the single place the function is genuinely meant to return.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the return is genuinely the last statement of the function, where leaving early was intended anyway.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: Yul and the leave statement; Slither documentation: return vs leave detector

detectors.title: A name contains a right-to-left override character
detectors.what_it_means: A string in the contract contains the control character U+202E, which reverses the text that follows it.
detectors.why_it_matters: The name is displayed to the user in the opposite order from how it is stored. A token whose name renders as the name of a well-known token is a substitution attack that needs no exploit at all -- it only needs the user to read the screen.
detectors.how_to_fix: Remove the character, and reject non-ASCII or control characters in any name, symbol or URI the contract displays.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the string is never shown to a user, for example an internal identifier or a hash.
detectors.references: Unicode technical standard #9: bidirectional behaviour; Slither documentation: right-to-left override detector

detectors.title: A state variable hides one from an abstract base
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a state variable with the same name as one in an abstract contract it inherits from.
detectors.why_it_matters: They are two different variables in two different storage slots. The base contract's functions -- including its access control -- read the base's variable, while the derived contract writes its own. The check passes on a value that is never updated.
detectors.how_to_fix: Rename one of the two so the inherited behaviour and the derived state are the same value.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the base's variable is never read and never meant to be shared.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: state variable shadowing; Slither documentation: shadowing from abstract contract detector

detectors.title: A state variable hides another one
detectors.what_it_means: Two state variables in the contract hierarchy share a name.
detectors.why_it_matters: The same failure as the abstract case, with the higher stakes: a function that checks owner may be checking a different variable from the one the rest of the contract writes. The access control reads a value that stays zero, or the write goes to a slot nobody reads.
detectors.how_to_fix: Rename the shadowing variable so that every function in the hierarchy reads and writes the same storage slot.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the shadowed variable is genuinely unused and never read.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: state variable shadowing; Slither documentation: state variable shadowing detector

detectors.title: A signed integer array is stored with a known compiler bug
detectors.what_it_means: The contract stores signed integers in a storage array using a compiler version that packs signed values incorrectly.
detectors.why_it_matters: The compiler miscomputes the packed slot of a signed value, so the array reads back a different number from the one written. Balances, indices and counters that are read back wrong are wrong on chain, permanently, and no amount of re-reading fixes them.
detectors.how_to_fix: Compile with a compiler version that does not have the bug, and use unsigned types where the value is never negative.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the affected array is never written, or where the compiler version in use is known to be free of the bug.
detectors.references: Solidity changelog: the signed storage array bug; Slither documentation: storage array detector

detectors.title: A value is compared with itself
detectors.what_it_means: The contract compares a variable with itself, so the comparison always has the same answer.
detectors.why_it_matters: The check that was written to stop something can never fail, and the branch that was written to do something is always taken. A guard written in the wrong order, or with the wrong variable on one side, looks like protection and provides none.
detectors.how_to_fix: Correct the comparison so that it compares the two values it was meant to compare, and check the branch that depends on it.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the comparison is genuinely about the same value, for example an assertion that a value is not NaN.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: tautological comparison detector

detectors.title: A condition is always true or always false
detectors.what_it_means: The contract's condition is decided at compile time.
detectors.why_it_matters: The condition on a branch is not a condition. Either the branch is unreachable, so code that was meant to handle a case never runs, or it is unconditional, so the code it was supposed to skip always runs.
detectors.how_to_fix: Replace the constant with the condition that was meant, or remove the branch and the code it guarded.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the constant is a deliberate compile-time switch with a comment explaining it.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: tautology detector

detectors.title: A value is written and then written again unread
detectors.what_it_means: The contract writes to a variable, and writes to it again before anything reads it.
detectors.why_it_matters: The first write is dead. That is nearly always a mistake: a limit that was set and then overwritten by a stale value, or a check that recorded a value the code no longer uses. The behaviour that was written is not the behaviour that runs.
detectors.how_to_fix: Read the first value before overwriting it, or remove the first write if it was not meant to survive.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the first write is to a variable that is only read later through storage rather than through the local slot.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: write after write detector

detectors.title: An assertion stands where a state change was expected
detectors.what_it_means: The contract uses assert to require a state change it should have made.
detectors.why_it_matters: The assert does not change anything: it only checks a condition and reverts when the condition fails. Whatever the contract meant to record -- a balance, a flag, a counter -- is never written, so the state after the call is not the state the code reads as if it had been updated.
detectors.how_to_fix: Perform the state change and then assert the condition that must hold afterwards.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the assert is a genuine sanity check on an input and no state change was intended.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: assert state change detector

detectors.title: A boolean is compared with a boolean constant
detectors.what_it_means: The contract compares a boolean with true or false.
detectors.why_it_matters: The comparison is decided at compile time on one side, so the branch is either always taken or never taken. It reads like a check and behaves like a constant, and it hides which of the two happened.
detectors.how_to_fix: Remove the constant comparison, or write the check against the value that is actually meant to be tested.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the comparison documents an invariant on purpose and the branch it guards is deliberately one-sided.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: comparison to boolean constant detector

detectors.title: A loop re-reads the length of a storage array
detectors.what_it_means: The contract's loop condition reads the length of a storage array on every iteration.
detectors.why_it_matters: Each read of a storage array's length is an SLOAD, which costs far more than a value in memory. A loop of a thousand iterations pays a thousand storage reads for a number that does not change.
detectors.how_to_fix: Read the length once into a local variable before the loop and use that.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless when the loop runs a small, bounded number of times, or when the array is in memory rather than in storage.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: storage arrays and gas costs; Slither documentation: cache array length detector

detectors.title: The Chainlink feed registry is consulted
detectors.what_it_means: The contract reads a price feed address from the Chainlink feed registry rather than holding the feed address itself.
detectors.why_it_matters: The registry is an external contract that can change what a feed address resolves to. The contract's price source is therefore decided by something outside the contract, and the decision can change between two calls.
detectors.how_to_fix: Hold the feed address in the contract's own storage, set by an administrator, and check the feed's code and decimals when it is set.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the registry is used only to read a feed that is already trusted by the rest of the protocol.
detectors.references: Chainlink documentation: feed registry; Slither documentation: chainlink feed registry detector

detectors.title: A state variable could have been a constant
detectors.what_it_means: The contract keeps a value in storage that is written once and never changes.
detectors.why_it_matters: Every read of that value costs an SLOAD and every deployment pays for storing it. The value can also be written later by whatever path reaches the setter, which is exactly the risk a constant removes.
detectors.how_to_fix: Declare it as a constant where it is fixed at compile time, or as an immutable where it is fixed at deployment.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the value is expected to be changed later by an administrator, in which case a setter with access control is the right shape.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: constant and immutable variables; Slither documentation: constable states detector

detectors.title: A deprecated Solidity standard is used
detectors.what_it_means: The contract uses a language or ABI feature that newer standards have deprecated.
detectors.why_it_matters: The feature still works, but the standard it came from has been replaced, and the replacement exists because the old one had a problem -- typically an encoding that can be ambiguous or a behaviour that was changed. The code carries that problem forward.
detectors.how_to_fix: Move to the current standard, and check the behaviour difference rather than only the syntax.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the deprecated feature is used in a way the deprecation note explicitly leaves unchanged, or where the contract must support an old compiler.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: what is deprecated; Slither documentation: deprecated standards detector

detectors.title: An ERC20 event parameter is not indexed
detectors.what_it_means: The contract emits a Transfer or Approval event with a parameter that is not marked indexed.
detectors.why_it_matters: The parameter is stored in the log data rather than in a topic, so a client that filters the log by that value has to read every log and decode it. Indexers cannot answer 'all transfers to this address' from the topics alone.
detectors.how_to_fix: Mark the parameter indexed when clients are expected to filter on it, and keep the event under the three-indexed-argument limit.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the parameter is never used as a filter -- a memo, for instance -- and the event is read in full by every consumer.
detectors.references: ERC-20 standard: events; Slither documentation: un-indexed ERC20 event parameters detector

detectors.title: An event does not record the value it changed
detectors.what_it_means: The contract changes a value but the event it emits for that change does not carry the new value.
detectors.why_it_matters: The log records that something happened without recording what it did. An indexer that reconstructs the contract's state from the logs cannot reconstruct this value, and the off-chain history diverges from the chain.
detectors.how_to_fix: Include the new value in the event, and emit it where the value changes rather than only where the function is called.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the value is already recoverable from another event or from a transaction field.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: missing events arithmetic detector

detectors.title: A public function could have been external
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a function public that could be external.
detectors.why_it_matters: A public function's arguments are copied into memory; an external one reads them from calldata. For a function with a large argument the copy is paid on every call, and the contract pays it out of the caller's gas.
detectors.how_to_fix: Declare it external when nothing calls it internally, and keep it public when it does.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless when the function is called internally, in which case public is required.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: data location and function visibility; Slither documentation: external function detector

detectors.title: State is initialised outside the constructor
detectors.what_it_means: The contract initialises state variables in an ordinary function rather than in the constructor.
detectors.why_it_matters: The contract starts in a state the constructor was supposed to define. A function that sets an owner or a fee can be called before anyone intends it to, and the state it leaves behind is one the deployment never had.
detectors.how_to_fix: Move the initialisation into the constructor, so the contract has a defined state from the moment it exists.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the function is itself protected and is meant to be called later, for example a delayed migration.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: constructors; Slither documentation: function initializing state variables detector

detectors.title: A unary operator is applied in a way that changes its meaning
detectors.what_it_means: The contract applies a unary operator to a value in a way that is not what it looks like -- typically a negation or a bitwise not on an unsigned value, or a negation of a subtraction.
detectors.why_it_matters: The value that comes out is not the value the expression appears to produce. On an unsigned type a negation wraps to a very large number rather than to a negative one, and a check built on that expression is a check that never holds the way it was meant to.
detectors.how_to_fix: Write the expression so that its type matches its intent, and compare against the value you actually expect.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the wrap-around is the intended behaviour and the surrounding code is written for unsigned types.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: arithmetic and types; Slither documentation: incorrect unary expression detector

detectors.title: A using-for statement has no matching library function
detectors.what_it_means: The contract attaches a library function to a type with using-for, but no function in that library matches the type.
detectors.why_it_matters: The call does not resolve, so the code either fails to compile or -- where the type is ambiguous -- resolves to a different function than the author intended, with a different meaning.
detectors.how_to_fix: Name a library function that actually takes the type, or drop the using-for directive.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the library does provide the function and Slither cannot see it because the library is generated or inherited.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: using-for; Slither documentation: incorrect using for detector

detectors.title: A deprecated Optimism predeploy or function is used
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls a predeploy or function on Optimism that has been deprecated.
detectors.why_it_matters: The call still succeeds but the behaviour behind it is on its way out, and the deprecation exists because something about it will change. A contract that depends on it inherits that change without deciding to.
detectors.how_to_fix: Move to the current interface, and check the deprecation notice for what exactly is changing.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the deprecated item is used on a path the contract does not exercise, or where the notice states the behaviour is unchanged for this use.
detectors.references: Optimism documentation: deprecations; Slither documentation: optimism deprecation detector

detectors.title: A statement has no effect
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains a statement that does not change anything.
detectors.why_it_matters: The statement reads like a step in the logic and does nothing. Often it is the remnant of a check that was removed, or an assignment whose value was already correct, and what remains is the belief that something was verified.
detectors.how_to_fix: Delete the statement, or restore the check it stands for.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the statement is a deliberate no-op for readability, which is rare and worth a comment.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: redundant statements detector

detectors.title: A variable hides a built-in name
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a variable whose name is also the name of a built-in, such as gas, now or msg.
detectors.why_it_matters: Inside that scope the built-in means the variable. A function that reads gas to measure the remaining gas reads the contract's own variable instead, and the measurement is whatever the contract last stored there.
detectors.how_to_fix: Rename the variable so the built-in keeps its meaning.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the built-in is never used in the same scope, or where the shadowing is deliberate and commented.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: globally available variables; Slither documentation: shadowing builtin detector

detectors.title: A local variable hides another local variable
detectors.what_it_means: The contract declares a local variable with the same name as another local variable in an outer scope.
detectors.why_it_matters: The inner declaration hides the outer one for the rest of the block. A value that was computed and carried in the outer variable is read as the inner one, which is usually zero, and the code does not fail -- it simply computes something else.
detectors.how_to_fix: Rename one of the variables so the two values stay distinguishable.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the two variables are never used in the same expression and the shadowing is obvious at a glance.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: scoping and shadowing; Slither documentation: shadowing local variable detector

detectors.title: A function is declared but does nothing
detectors.what_it_means: The contract contains a function with an empty body.
detectors.why_it_matters: The function exists in the interface and can be called, but it does nothing. A caller that believes the function performed the action -- registering, approving, cancelling -- sees a successful transaction and no state change.
detectors.how_to_fix: Implement the function, or make it revert explicitly so the caller learns it is not available.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the function is an interface stub that the contract never exposes, or where it is deliberately a no-op that the documentation states.
detectors.references: Slither documentation: unimplemented functions detector

detectors.title: A constructor calls a function pointer that was never set
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls a function pointer in the constructor before the pointer has been given a value.
detectors.why_it_matters: The call goes to the zero address, which succeeds and does nothing -- or reverts, depending on the target. Either way the constructor's initialisation is incomplete, and the contract is deployed in a state its code never describes.
detectors.how_to_fix: Set the pointer before it is called, and check that it is not the zero address at the point of use.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the pointer is set earlier in the same constructor and Slither cannot see the ordering through a helper.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: function types; Slither documentation: uninitialized function pointer detector

detectors.title: A state variable is never read
detectors.what_it_means: The contract stores a value and never reads it back.
detectors.why_it_matters: The slot is written and never used. Often the variable was meant to be read -- a fee that should be applied, a limit that should be enforced, a flag that should gate something -- and the check that would read it was never written.
detectors.how_to_fix: Either use the variable where it was meant to be used, or remove it and the storage slot it occupies.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the variable exists for future versions or for external tooling that reads storage directly.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: state variables; Slither documentation: unused state variable detector

detectors.title: The contract reads its own variable through an external call
detectors.what_it_means: The contract reads one of its own state variables by calling itself through this.
detectors.why_it_matters: The read is an external call: it costs more gas and it can be re-entered, so the read happens at a moment the caller chose rather than at the moment the code intended.
detectors.how_to_fix: Read the storage variable directly instead of going through this.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the value must be read as an external call for a specific reason, which is rare enough to deserve a comment.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: the this keyword; Slither documentation: variable read using this detector

detectors.title: A variable is used before it is declared
detectors.what_it_means: The contract uses a local variable before the point where it is declared.
detectors.why_it_matters: The name resolves to a different variable -- usually an outer one, or a parameter -- so the value the code reads is not the value the author had in mind. The compiler's own scope rules are what make the mistake possible in the first place.
detectors.how_to_fix: Declare the variable before it is used, and rename any variable it hides.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the intended variable is the one that resolves, and the declaration order was chosen for readability rather than by mistake.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: scoping; Slither documentation: variable scope detector

detectors.title: A constructor is called but not implemented
detectors.what_it_means: The contract calls a constructor that has no implementation.
detectors.why_it_matters: The call succeeds and does nothing, so the initialisation the call was supposed to perform never happens. The contract is deployed with whatever state it had before, which is usually empty.
detectors.how_to_fix: Implement the constructor, or remove the call so it is clear the initialisation was never intended.
detectors.false_positive_patterns: Harmless where the constructor is an inherited one whose body Slither cannot see, or where the base's constructor is the one that does the work.
detectors.references: Solidity documentation: constructors; Slither documentation: constructor not implemented detector
